processing: The upper leaves and flowers of the shrub, Dasiphora fruticosa, are dried in shade; the material can be brewed after about a week and a half to two weeks. Some people wilt and roll the leaves, then dry or lightly roast them at about 60 °C.
harvest_season: Gathered from early summer until late autumn.
appearance_dry: Small silvery-green leaf fragments with thin stems and sometimes bits of yellow flower.
appearance_liquor: Little is recorded; as with other dried leaf herbs, expect a clear golden-amber cup.
appearance_wet: Soft greenish leaflets with stem pieces.
taste_profile: A plain dried brew is said to resemble green tea, and the rolled and roasted version good black tea.

brewing.notes: About a tablespoon per glass of boiling water, steeped around 10 minutes.

vintage_note: Sold without vintage, by weight or in herbal mixes, and usually as a dried herb. Bear in mind that the name covers a shrub also planted widely in gardens, so ask for the source of the material; ornamental plants may have been treated.
description:
Kuril tea is a drink from Dasiphora fruticosa, a hardy flowering shrub of cool and subarctic regions around the northern hemisphere, often growing high in the mountains. Gardeners know it as shrubby cinquefoil, and older books file it under Potentilla fruticosa.

The upper leaves and flowers are usually simply dried, though some people roll and lightly roast them. The name suggests one place, but the plant is far more widespread than the Kuril Islands, and folk use is reported from Kamchatka, Sakhalin and Western Siberia.

Tasting notes are few: the plain brew is said to resemble green tea, the rolled and roasted one black tea.

A lot of what is written about it is about health rather than taste. Read those claims with care: folk use is well recorded, but it is not evidence that the tea treats anything.
history:
The plant has a long record in Tibetan and Mongolian medicine, where decoctions and infusions were used for stomach and intestinal infections. People on Kamchatka drank leaf infusions for acute stomach pain, and on Sakhalin decoctions of the whole plant were used against tuberculosis.

Those are records of folk medicine, not of daily tea drinking. One popular account says the name comes from people of the Kuril Islands and the Far East brewing the leaves in the 18th and 19th centuries. In folk speech it is also called mogutchka.
